abstract: Heterogeneous dynamics, including phenomena such as superspreading and clustering, is a hallmark of many infectious diseases. A key challenge lies in identifying observables that constrain heterogeneous dynamics. We here adapt the technique of turbulence decomposition from fluid dynamics to extract scale-dependent fluctuation spectra and correlation functions from disaggregated epidemiological data as a probe of population heterogeneity. To investigate possible explanations for the observed heterogeneities during the COVID-19 winter wave in Germany in 2020/21, we calculate synthetic observables using the new network-based simulation code \textsc{Epimetheus} for an idealized structured population. The code can flexibly incorporate clustering, heterogeneous connectivity and susceptibility, superspreading as well as temporal modulations of transmission risk and factors like waning of immunity and vaccination. A qualitative comparison of simulated and observed fluctuation spectra and correlation functions as well as the secondary attack rate and the overdispersion indicates that both clustering and variations of susceptibility across population substructures of all scales are required to produce the observed dynamics. Combined with heterogeneous connectivity, it is likely that self-limiting effects would have limited the winter outbreak to $0.2\texttt{-}0.35$ of the population without further behavioral changes after the autumn of 2020. A uniform population-wide reduction of transmission risk alone does not adequately explain the observed heterogeneities. Further analysis of the relative contributions and interplay of interventions and self-limiting effects on COVID-19 disease dynamics is required. We outline avenues towards a better integration of heterogeneity in models for predicting infectious disease dynamics and diagnosing effects of interventions.
